summary: Gives sample inputs and expected outputs for HMAC built with the MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions. Implementers can run these test cases to check that their code computes message authentication codes correctly. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is an answer key. You do the math with your own program, then compare with the key to see whether your program is correct.

subtitle: Answer key to verify implementations of HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1.

tldr.problem: Implementers of HMAC message authentication codes need a way to verify that their code produces correct results and is interoperable with other implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides seven test cases each for HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1, specifying the key, data input, expected digest output, and in some cases truncated digest output. Implementations can run their code with these test inputs and check if outputs match the expected values.
tldr.outcome: This conformance test document allows developers to verify correctness and ensures interoperability between different implementations of HMAC-based authentication.

today: RFC 2202 is an Informational document that remains the standard reference for testing HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 implementations.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 2202 provides test cases for verifying the correctness of HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1 implementations. HMAC (Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication) is a construction method that builds message authentication codes using existing hash functions. HMAC-MD5 uses the MD5 hash function, while HMAC-SHA-1 uses the SHA-1 hash function. Both constructs are used by IPsec and other protocols to authenticate messages and verify they have not been altered in transit.

The test cases are cross-verified by independent implementations from NIST and IBM Research, ensuring an implementation that produces matching results should be interoperable with other similar implementations.
sections.eli5: HMAC is a method for using a secret password to create a unique fingerprint of a message. This document gives examples you can use to check if your fingerprint method is working correctly.

sections.title: How to Use the Test Cases
sections.content:
Each test case specifies a key (in hexadecimal or as an ASCII string), the data to authenticate, and the expected digest (checksum). To use these test cases, implement HMAC according to the HMAC specification, run it with the test key and data, and verify the output matches the expected digest. If all test cases pass, the implementation is likely correct.

The test case values are given in hexadecimal notation (prefixed by 0x) or as ASCII character strings in double quotes. If a value is an ASCII string, HMAC computation does not include the trailing null character. Some test cases also provide a truncated digest output, showing how to keep only the more significant (leftmost) bits when a shorter authentication code is needed.
sections.eli5: For each test case, you write the key and message into your program, let it calculate, and check if you get the same answer shown in the test case.

sections.title: HMAC-MD5 Test Cases
sections.content:
RFC 2202 provides seven test cases for HMAC-MD5. Test case 1 uses a 16-byte key and the 8-byte message "Hi There", expecting the digest 0x9294727a3638bb1c13f48ef8158bfc9d. Test case 2 uses a 4-byte ASCII key "Jefe" with a longer message. Test case 3 uses a 16-byte key of repeated bytes with data repeated 50 times. Test cases 4 through 7 provide additional test inputs with various key and data lengths, including one case (case 5) that demonstrates digest truncation to 96 bits.

All HMAC-MD5 digests are 16 bytes (128 bits) when not truncated, as MD5 produces a 128-bit hash output.
sections.eli5: The test cases show different situations: short messages, long messages, short keys, long keys, and cases where you only keep part of the answer. Your implementation should handle all of these correctly.

sections.title: HMAC-SHA-1 Test Cases
sections.content:
Seven parallel test cases for HMAC-SHA-1 are provided, mirroring the structure of the HMAC-MD5 test cases. Test case 1 uses a 20-byte key with "Hi There", expecting the digest 0xb617318655057264e28bc0b6fb378c8ef146be00. The test cases cover similar scenarios to HMAC-MD5: short and long messages, short and long keys, and truncation examples (case 5 shows truncation to 96 bits).

All HMAC-SHA-1 digests are 20 bytes (160 bits) when not truncated, since SHA-1 produces a 160-bit hash output.
sections.eli5: HMAC-SHA-1 is very similar to HMAC-MD5 but uses a different underlying hash function. The test cases follow the same pattern but produce longer answers because SHA-1 is larger than MD5.
